lines: Thousands of sellers all share one single warehouse here.
One seller's own nightly report scans the entire fact table, and every other seller's dashboard genuinely slows to a crawl because of it.
At month end, finance asks what each individual seller actually costs, and the honest answer turns out to be: the warehouse is mostly idle, and there's simply no per-seller number at all.
Which two controls, if they'd been designed in right from the start, would have actually stopped that slowdown and produced the number finance was asking for?
answer: A bigger warehouse still lets one single tenant consume the entire thing, and it still produces absolutely no per-tenant number on its own.
What genuinely helps is a per-tenant limit on heavy queries, paired with a metering view that attributes cost back to each individual query.

lines: Shared tables with row-level security sit at the cheap end: weakest blast-radius containment, but far and away the cheapest option.
A schema or catalog per tenant sits in the middle.
An account or project per tenant is the strongest option, and also by far the most expensive, each one priced here for both a small and a genuinely large tenant count.
A regulated tenant and a separately noisy tenant each get pushed up by exactly one rung from that cheap default.
Each push happens because of one specific, named constraint, never as some blanket upgrade applied to every single tenant at once.
One single tenant's own lane spikes up to many times its normal load.
With no control at all in place, every neighbour's own latency climbs right along with it.
With a real quota and a fairness rule actually in place, those same neighbours stay completely flat instead.
That exact same spike, now split three entirely different ways.

An equal share ends up starving a large, perfectly legitimate tenant. A weighted share instead favors whoever happens to pay more. And burst-with-credit lets a short spike through just fine, while still capping anything sustained.
A tenant stored under its own schema, or its own key, erases genuinely cheaply: one single drop, one key deleted, done.
That exact same tenant sitting in a shared table instead needs a full scan and rewrite — and this erasure cost was actually already decided, way back at the isolation choice itself.
A single bill splits apart into per-tenant slices, straight from the engine's own metering view.
Plus one grey "idle and shared" remainder that none of those slices actually cover.
Three separate policy cards decide what happens to it next: charge it proportionally, charge it as a flat fee, or simply absorb it entirely.
A priced isolation ladder. A fairness rule that genuinely decides who ends up getting starved.
An erasure cost that was already paid for, back at the isolation choice.
And one metered bill that stays honest about its own leftover remainder.
One more, to really use this for real: the marketplace grows all the way out to ten times its current tenant count.
The cheapest rung's own per-tenant cost barely moves at all.
But the metering view's own overhead genuinely starts showing up as a real line on the bill. What's actually the next bottleneck here?
answer: The rung choice itself was driven by one named constraint, never by tenant count alone, so moving every single tenant up multiplies cost for tenants that triggered no constraint whatsoever.
A metering view carries a perfectly real cost of its own, and that cost scales directly with query count, so it can genuinely become the next thing this design has to watch closely.
